description: The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) achieves O(N) complexity for N-body force evaluation by using multipole expansions to represent far-field contributions and local expansions for near-field. Unlike Barnes-Hut which evaluates each particle independently, FMM translates multipole expansions between tree levels (M2M, M2L, L2L operators), amortizing the cost of far-field computation.
mathematical_formalization: Multipole expansion of potential at distance R from cluster center: Phi(r) = sum_{l=0}^{p} sum_{m=-l}^{l} M_lm * Y_lm(theta, phi) / r^{l+1}. Translation operators: M2M (shift multipole center), M2L (convert multipole to local expansion), L2L (shift local center). Total cost: O(p^2 * N) for expansion order p.
analogical_connections: Fourier transforms decompose signals into frequency components; FMM decomposes force fields into multipole components at different spatial scales
Wavelet multiresolution analysis: both FMM and wavelets represent fields at multiple scales with local basis functions
DNS caching hierarchy: root servers aggregate information (M2M), distribute to local resolvers (M2L, L2L)
implementation_hypothesis: For a minimal gravity sim, implement a 2D FMM with monopole + dipole terms (p=1). Build the tree, compute M2M upward, M2L at each level, L2L downward, then evaluate local expansions at leaf nodes. Compare with Barnes-Hut for same accuracy.
experiment_seed: Benchmark FMM vs Barnes-Hut vs direct summation for N={10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6}. Measure wall-clock time and relative force error. FMM should show O(N) scaling vs O(N log N) for Barnes-Hut.
